RagShortTexts: Fur cargo needs checks of dryness, wear and count; marks help identify a bale.
Inspection, witnesses and handovers matter; a lead seal alone cannot prove quality or title.

Variants.Content:
Furs reaching Novgorod pass through hunting, preparation, buying and repeated handling. Species matters, but so do the coat, damage and keeping. Damp skins spoil inside a bale and damage others, making drying and rain protection essential. Buyers may open part of the cargo to distinguish whole skins, pieces and mixtures rather than value everything by the best visible skin.

Knots, seals and owners’ marks help identify a package, but substitution, shortages and uncertain responsibility remain possible. An intact mark does not prove the skins stayed dry or that a suspicious seller owns them. Porters, stores and recipients need to know the agreement, including how an inspected bale is tied again.
Merchant leaders need trusted witnesses for inspection, storage and claims. Arbitrary opening and exactions by guards enter the price of future trade.
Escorts watch bindings and covers and count packages at relief. Reporting a broken mark immediately avoids carrying both the problem and suspicion to the destination.
Transport and intermediaries reduce hunters’ returns. Sound preservation helps bargaining, but drying furs competes for household shelter and labour.
